item.title: New audio undercuts Dems who defended Biden, slammed Hur after classified docs report revealed memory loss
item.description: Newly publicized audio tapes from Robert Hur's classified documents investigation prove his report's claims of Biden struggling to recall names and dates during 2017 interviews.
item.content:encoded:
After special counsel Robert Hur’s 2023 investigation and the subsequent report into former President Joe Biden’s retention of classified documents, Democrats rushed to defend the 46th president from his characterization that Biden was an "elderly man with a poor memory."

The left-wing's narrative surrounding Biden's mental cognition — especially as he was running for re-election against President Donald Trump — is now crumbling after audio tapes from the investigation were revealed Monday night.

Prominent Democrats lined up to defend Biden when the initial report was released in 2024, many using the same line that Hur's report was "gratuitous." Then-Vice President Kamala Harris was chief among the chorus of defenders, saying that the report was "inaccurate and inappropriate."

"The way that the president’s demeanor in that report was characterized could not be more wrong on the facts," she told reporters at an event in Washington at the time. She also said the report was "clearly politically motivated, gratuitous." Months later, Biden dropped out of the presidential race and was replaced on the ticket by his No. 2 without a primary election to decide his replacement.

BIDEN'S HUR INTERVIEW TAPES COULD NOW GO PUBLIC AFTER HIS ATTORNEYS WAVE WHITE FLAG

"What everyone will soon realize is that this is a Republican special counsel who completely went out of his way to editorialize, to include material in his report that is unnecessary and irrelevant to what he was tasked with doing," Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., piled on in comments to ABC at the time.

Hur's appointment was nonpartisan.

In 2023, Hur was investigating Biden for retaining classified information. At the center of the investigation were audio tapes of Biden from interviews with his "Promise Me, Dad" memoir ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, from 2016 and 2017.

Hur's report concluded that Biden did, in fact, retain classified documents, but that prosecuting him might not lead to a conviction, because he could be viewed "as a sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory."

"Mr. Biden's memory was significantly limited, both during his recorded interviews with the ghostwriter in 2017 and in his interview with our office in 2023," the report said.

BIDEN’S FIGHT TO KEEP HUR INTERVIEW TAPES UNDER WRAPS SUFFERS FRESH COURT BLOW

After a prolonged legal battle during which Biden sought to keep the audio tapes private, a nonprofit called the Oversight Project obtained them via public records requests. The damning tapes reveal Biden's inability to remember basic names and dates.

In one instance, on April 24, 2017, Biden struggled to recall the names of two economic advisers.

"I’ll think of his name," said Biden, who at the time was a private citizen and former vice president. "I should write the names down because I keep forgetting them."

There was then a long pause before Zwonitzer prompted Biden by saying Alan Krueger’s name.

BIDEN SCORES TEMPORARY COURT VICTORY AS TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE DELAYS RELEASE OF HUR INVESTIGATION MATERIALS

In another instance, when trying to recall a memorial he attended for a fallen service member, Biden forgot the date of the service and name of the deceased.

"I think I went to that memorial service in Wilmington. It says [REDACTED] December the 4th, but I don't -- I know what this means. Memorial service -- [REDACTED] gets names really f---ed up," said Biden.

"So it says memorial service for [REDACTED]. I don't think her name was [REDACTED]. Or I forget [REDACTED]."

The interviews were marked by consistent lapses in memory.

But in 2024, that didn't stop Democrats from accusing Hur of being a partisan activist who intentionally tried to tarnish Biden and his chances in a rematch against Trump.

Andrew Weissman, a former general counsel to the FBI, cried foul on MSNBC.

"That is not the role of the Department of Justice ... to talk about your memory today — irrelevant, it is gratuitous," he reportedly said. "And it is also exactly what you're not supposed to do, which is putting your thumb on the scale that could have political repercussions."

Ian Sams, a spokesperson for Biden's general counsel, said at the time that the report was "gratuitous."

"When you are the first special counsel in history not to indict anybody, there is pressure to criticize and to make, you know, statements that maybe in otherwise you wouldn't make," Sams reportedly said.

"I think this issue of age is already out there, and when November comes, it’s going to be a choice between two people," said Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., told POLITICO. "I was with a congressional leadership about two weeks ago, and no one walked out of that meeting, saying, ‘Oh, my God, it was like he wasn’t in charge.’"

Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., who at the time had just spent a day traveling with Biden, insisted that he was, "at the very top of his game, all the way through it, both in private and in person."

Later in 2024, Biden was yanked from the top of the presidential ticket after an embarrassing debate performance against then-candidate Donald Trump, which showcased his apparent mental decline.

Harris, serving as vice president at the time, was then coronated as the party's presidential nominee despite never winning a primary. When she ran in 2020, Harris never made it to the primaries, dropping out on December 3, 2019, months before the first elections took place.

A Biden spokesperson ducked the former president's memory in a statement to CBS.

"President Biden's conversations for a book a decade ago that discussed his late son are private, and were provided to the Department of Justice on the express condition they stay that way," TJ Ducklo told the outlet. "Reversing course and making them public is just the latest example of this Administration weaponizing the DOJ for political retribution."

"It's wrong, and while President Biden disagrees with today's decision, he also respects the courts and the vital role an independent judiciary plays in a healthy democracy."

item.title: Kamala Harris backs US Senate candidate who replaced Graham Platner: 'I know what it is like'
item.description: Former Vice President Kamala Harris declared her support for Maine Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson, drawing a parallel between his run and her 2024 presidential bid.
item.content:encoded:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris backed Democratic Maine U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson.

"I know what it is like to step up to the plate with a short runway to Election Day. Troy will have just 101 days between his nomination for Senate and when voters in Maine will cast their ballots," Harris said in a Monday fundraising email.

Harris was tapped as the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee after incumbent President Joe Biden dropped out in the wake of a widely-panned debate performance against then-former President Donald Trump.

MAINE DEMOCRATS CROWN TROY JACKSON AS PLATNER REPLACEMENT AS FRESH SCRUTINY CLOUDS SENATE RESET

Jackson, a former state senator who ran unsuccessfully in the Democratic Maine gubernatorial primary this year, was tapped as the U.S. Senate nominee at the Maine Democratic Party's U.S. Senate Nominating Convention on Saturday. The general election will be on Nov. 3.

Graham Platner, who won the 2026 Maine Democratic U.S. Senate primary last month, dropped out of the race earlier this month in the face of a rape allegation, though he had asserted, "Any accusation of non-consensual behavior is categorically false."

Fox News Digital reached out to Jackson's campaign on Tuesday.

BERNIE SANDERS REJECTS REGRET OVER EARLY GRAHAM PLATNER SUPPORT DESPITE 'WARNING SIGNS'

Jackson is challenging long-serving incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has been in office since 1997.

Collins campaign spokeswoman Blake Kernen said in a statement to Fox News on Monday that Harris "knows exactly what he’s going through."

FORMER PLATNER ALLY TROY JACKSON LOCKS DOWN DELEGATES AS TOP RIVALS FOR DEMOCRATIC SENATE NOMINATION DROP OUT

"Nice to see two people bond over their shared passion for completely bypassing primary voters," the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) noted in a Monday statement to Fox News.

The Associated Press, Fox News' Alexis McAdams and Fox News' Jessica Sonkin contributed to this report.

item.title: Shaquille O'Neal offers rebuttal for NBA fans claiming LeBron James is 'ring chasing' by joining Sixers
item.description: Shaquille O'Neal defends LeBron James against ring chaser criticism, comparing the Philadelphia 76ers move to his own final season with Boston Celtics.
item.content:encoded:
It goes without saying that LeBron James would like to win another NBA title before retiring, which is the same goal that every single player in the Association has. That fact hasn't slowed down the criticism of James' decision to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers, with many labeling him a "ring chaser" for taking his talents to Philly.

James, who will turn 42 in December, has four NBA championship rings to his name, having won them with three different teams. It's very easy to argue that his choice to join the Sixers as opposed to other suitors such as the Miami Heat, Cleveland Cavaliers, and Golden State Warriors does give him the best and perhaps easiest path to pick up another title, which leads back to the ring-chasing title he's picked up since making his decision.

If we're honest, James would have been labeled a ring chaser no matter what franchise he signed with simply based on his age and the fact that he's on the tail end of his career.

PHILADELPHIA ATHLETES, INCLUDING NEW TEAMMATES, REACT TO LEBRON JAMES JOINING 76ERS: 'WELCOME TO THE CITY'

Basketball Hall of Famer Shaquille O'Neal knows a thing or two about carrying around the same label of ring chaser after joining the Boston Celtics in the final season of his career. James receiving similar treatment before suiting up for the Sixers doesn't exactly sit well with him, however.

"I don't like y'all calling my man a ring chaser," O'Neal said, referring to James, during a recent appearance on "The Stephen A. Smith Show."

"It's funny to me that people that don't have rings to say 'Oh, he's a ring chaser.' No, he's continuous chasing, he's chasing the chance to continue to be great, to continue to add legacy to his book.

"When this thing is over, it's over, you can't come back. Once you retire, once your body says it can't go no more, it's over. This guy feels he has two or three years left, why not try and get another championship? I did it, I did it with Boston. I won three in a row and then won one in Miami. At the end of my career, let me go play with Paul [Pierce] and KG (Kevin Garnett) and see if I can win one."

THE 76ERS JUMP TO BETTING FAVORITE OUT EAST AFTER LEBRON JAMES TAKES HIS TALENTS TO PHILADELPHIA

James will be teaming up alongside Joel Embiid, Jaylen Brown, and Tyrese Maxey in Philadelphia, which could evolve into a certified four-headed monster in the Eastern Conference.

The most important word in the previous sentence, however, is 'could.'

Ring chaser, or 'continious chaser' as O'Neal put it, the labels and even the predictions don't matter at this point. The only thing that does matter is what James and the Sixers do come April of next year when the postseason starts.

item.title: Wearable patch vibrates when danger is nearby
item.description: NC State researchers built a solar-powered wearable patch with six sensors that vibrates against your skin using distinct haptic alerts for each hazard.
item.content:encoded:
Your phone can warn you about bad weather or heavy traffic. However, some dangers cannot wait for you to notice a notification. A hazardous gas may already surround you. Contaminated water may look perfectly normal. By the time you unlock your phone and check an alert, you could have already spent valuable time near the threat.

Researchers at North Carolina State University have developed a wearable patch that takes the phone out of that warning process. The device detects environmental hazards, then vibrates directly against your skin.

Different vibration patterns tell you which hazard the patch detected. Meanwhile, a related version gives robots their own form of chemical awareness.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

SELF-DRESSING CLOTHES COULD HELP OLDER ADULTS

The square patch is slightly smaller than a driver's license. That makes it compact enough to attach to clothing or place directly against the skin. Inside, a microcontroller acts as the patch's brain. A small battery powers the system. Six sensors monitor the surrounding environment for potential hazards.

The researchers designed the sensors to detect threats in the air and contaminants in water. Examples include dangerous gases and heavy metals. Once the patch detects a hazard, a tiny actuator creates a vibration against your skin. That physical alert could be harder to overlook than another phone notification.

"If you're coming into contact with a hazardous substance, you need to know as quickly as possible," said Erim Uzunoğlu, the paper's first author and a Ph.D. student at NC State. The research appears in the scientific journal Device .

Environmental sensors already exist. Many can send a warning to your smartphone. However, that approach depends on you noticing the alert. Your phone could be in a pocket, buried in a bag or silenced during work.

A physical vibration removes that extra step. The warning reaches your body as soon as the sensor detects a potential threat. Still, the researchers found that adding a small vibrating motor was not enough. The sensation had to feel strong and distinct without becoming uncomfortable.

To solve that problem, they created tiny textured surfaces between the motor and the skin. These surfaces resemble miniature patterns of raised bumps. By changing the size and spacing of the bumps, the team adjusted how each vibration felt. As a result, the alert became easier to notice. The design could prove helpful in loud environments where an audible alarm might disappear into the background.

The patch does not use the same buzzing sensation for every warning. Instead, it produces a separate haptic sequence for each hazard. One pattern might signal a dangerous gas. Another could warn about a contaminant in water.

This creates a small tactile language between the patch and the person wearing it. Therefore, you may understand the type of threat without checking a display. In proof-of-concept testing, the patch successfully detected the targeted substances. It also triggered the appropriate vibration immediately.

However, people would need time to learn what each pattern means. Clear training would become especially important in workplaces where several hazards may be present.

A wearable safety device offers little protection when its battery dies halfway through the day. To reduce that risk, the researchers placed thin-film photovoltaic cells on the patch's exterior. These cells collect solar energy while someone wears the device.

The solar cells work alongside the internal battery. At the same time, the sensors use relatively little power. During testing, that combination kept the device operating for around 24 hours. That running time could cover a full work shift. However, real-world performance would depend on sunlight, sensor activity and how someone wears the patch.

COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

As the team developed the wearable patch, the researchers began considering another question. Could a robot use the same tactile warning system? That idea led to an electronic skin, also called e-skin.

The robotic version places the sensor patch over a piezoelectric layer. When the patch vibrates, that movement creates an electrical signal. The robot can read the signal and identify the vibration pattern. It can then respond to the detected hazard without waiting for a wireless message.

During testing, researchers placed the e-skin on quadrupedal robots. When the robots detected chemical hazards, they changed direction and followed a safer route. This system could help robots explore locations that may be unsafe for people. It could also let a machine respond when wireless connections become unreliable.

Most robots rely heavily on cameras and digital instructions to understand their surroundings. Yet a camera cannot always identify a dangerous gas or invisible contaminant. The e-skin gives a robot another way to sense risk. More importantly, it turns the chemical warning into a physical signal within the robot's body.

That direct connection could support faster decisions. The robot would not need to transmit sensor data to a remote computer before responding. For example, a robot could inspect an industrial site while watching for leaks. It could then stop or change direction when it encounters a dangerous substance.

However, this work remains at the proof-of-concept stage. Researchers will need to test the system across harsher conditions before it can support high-risk missions.

Many experimental wearables rely on highly specialized components. Those custom parts can increase costs and slow production. In contrast, the researchers built most of this patch and e-skin with components that are already available. Only a few elements required custom engineering. That could make the technology easier to scale.

The sensor array is also modular. Developers could remove sensors that are unnecessary for a certain environment. They could then add sensors for hazards tied to a specific job or location. A water-quality worker would need a different setup than someone inspecting an area for chemical leaks.

You cannot buy this wearable hazard detection patch yet. Still, the research shows how safety alerts could move beyond screens and speakers. A vibration against your skin may reach you faster than a notification on your phone. That could become especially valuable when every second affects your exposure.

The technology may eventually help people who work near chemicals or inspect questionable water supplies. It could also support emergency teams entering places where the air may be unsafe. However, several questions remain. Researchers must determine how the patch performs after repeated wear and exposure to harsh conditions. They will also need to reduce false alarms and make each vibration easy to recognize. Comfort will play a role too. A safety patch only works when people are willing to wear it throughout the day.

NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL

A warning can only protect you when it reaches you in time. This wearable patch brings the alert directly to your skin instead of relying on a phone that you may never check. The separate vibration patterns are especially clever. They could tell you which danger is nearby before you even look at a screen. Meanwhile, the robot e-skin gives machines a physical way to recognize chemical threats and move away from them. That could eventually keep people farther from hazardous areas. The next challenge will be turning a successful laboratory prototype into something durable, comfortable and dependable enough for daily use.

item.title: Fetterman strongly supports the filibuster as Trump urges Senate Republicans to scrap it
item.description: Democratic Sen. John Fetterman supports the filibuster while President Donald Trump is pressuring Senate Republicans to scrap the filibuster.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., expressed strong support for the filibuster in a Monday opinion piece, acknowledging that he has reversed his position on the issue since his 2022 campaign.

President Donald Trump on Monday was pressuring Senate Republicans to nix the filibuster.

"When Democrats had the presidency and a majority in both chambers, they were frustrated with the 60-vote threshold needed to advance legislation. Senate Democrats attempted to end the filibuster to push through President Joe Biden’s agenda — an effort I fully supported during my 2022 campaign," Fetterman wrote in a Washington Post opinion piece.

"Halfway through my first term, I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it," he noted.

FETTERMAN TROLLS THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA AS ISRAEL KILLS HAMAS TERRORISTS: 'CRY HARDER'

"The rule is a critical line of defense that prevents President Donald Trump from having a fill-in-the-blank government with new laws, deregulation or procedures of its choosing," he wrote.

The president issued Truth Social posts on Monday advocating for Republicans to scrap the filibuster.

"John Thune should not allow the United States Senate to 'leave town' until it passes The Save America Act or, far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER, where Republicans can then quickly pass everything they ever dreamed of, including a full and deep throated SAVE AMERICA ACT, the Budget, and the ever looming Debt Ceiling disaster, 1929! The Dumocrats will do it on day one, and can’t believe how lucky they got with this Senate leadership. Remember, stupidity always brings LOSING & DEATH!" Trump wrote.

DEMS CLASH OVER AIPAC MONEY, 'OGRE' ATTACK AND ELECTABILITY DURING CRUCIAL SENATE DEBATE

In another post, he declared, "Whichever Party Terminates the Filibuster FIRST will be the Party that survives and thrives. If the Dumocrats win this race, however, America will rapidly become nothing more than a Third World Nation!"

The three-fifths threshold required for cloture to end a filibuster means that Senate Republicans, even with their 53-seat majority, cannot get to 60 votes without Democrats — the procedural hurdle prevents advancing most legislation with a simple majority.

REPUBLICANS SAY THEY'D WELCOME FETTERMAN AS GOP EYES BIGGER SENATE MAJORITY

"The one thing that has stopped many unpopular policies since the beginning of 2025 isn’t the Democrats — it is the filibuster," Fetterman wrote in his opinion piece.

item.title: Kyle Busch's widow opens up about grief and loneliness in emotional social media posts
item.description: Samantha Busch shared emotional Instagram posts revealing the unbearable loneliness she faces each night, two months after Kyle Busch died from sepsis.
item.content:encoded:
It's been more than two months since Kyle Busch's sudden death, and understandably, it is not getting any easier for his widow.

In a series of Instagram Stories, Samantha Busch said some nights without her late husband are "almost unbearable."

"You’re still the last thing I see when I close my eyes and the first thing when I wake up," Busch posted on Sunday along with photos of the couple by her bedside.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"In the evenings when the kids go to bed the silence and loneliness is almost unbearable. I sleep tucked on my side of the bed with a body pillow and his shirt pretending he’s still next to me. I hate it so much that his shirt doesn’t smell like him anymore."

Busch died on May 21 after severe pneumonia turned into sepsis, sandwiched between the Coca-Cola 600 and his final victory.

The two-time NASCAR champion collapsed during a simulator session ahead of the Coca-Cola 600 and was rushed to the hospital. He died the next day.

Busch was a two-time Cup champion and undoubtedly a future Hall of Famer. He had been in the Cup Series since 2004, making 762 career starts with 63 wins.

KYLE BUSCH'S SON SUFFERS HEARTBREAK IN EMOTIONAL RETURN TO RACING AFTER FATHER'S STUNNING DEATH

The 41-year-old won the championship in 2015 and 2019, and had 234 victories across all three NASCAR national series.

Busch is the all-time record-holder for wins in both the NASCAR O'Reilly Auto Parts Series (102) and the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series (69).

Busch's 234th and final NASCAR win came at Dover one week before his death, when he led 147 laps in a dominating Truck Series victory.

"You never know when the last one is," Busch said after the win.

Busch's last Cup Series win came in June 2023. While he struggled for much of this season, he did start on the pole in February's Daytona 500 and was coming off a season-best finish of eighth four weeks ago at Watkins Glen.

OutKick's Zach Dean contributed to this report.

item.title: GOP senator unveils BOASBERG Act to stop 'rogue' judges from handpicking Trump cases
item.description: Sen. Eric Schmitt's BOASBERG Act would require random assignment of federal cases and bar chief judges from influencing who hears high-profile disputes.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican is planning to curb so-called "rogue" judges, and he is using one of President Donald Trump’s greatest foils in the judicial branch as the launching point.

Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., is planning to introduce the Blocking Overt Attempts at Shopping By Enforcing Randomization Guidelines Act in an attempt to curb judge shopping in federal cases. The bill, shortened to the BOASBERG Act, is named after U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, one of Trump’s main antagonists on the bench.

Schmitt’s legislation, first obtained by Fox News Digital, would broadly require that federal cases be randomly assigned in a bid to limit the ability of judges and litigants to influence who gets to hear and oversee a case.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP'S ELECTION ORDER AS SAVE AMERICA ACT FIGHT INTENSIFIES

"Judge Boasberg is the poster child for a rogue judge and exposed serious loopholes in our judicial system," Schmitt said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Randomly assigning cases among judges ensures the American people can have confidence in the impartiality of our courts."

Schmitt’s legislation adds several guardrails to the selection process for federal cases and gives courts 120 days after enactment to implement them.

It would require the random assignment of federal civil cases, prohibit chief judges from influencing case assignments, require courts to publicly disclose their case assignment practices, create penalties for meddling with or manipulating the assignment process, and require the random reassignment of a case if the Supreme Court intervenes in a ruling.

DC APPEALS COURT ORDERS JUDGE BOASBERG TO HALT TRUMP CONTEMPT PROBE OVER DEPORTATION FLIGHTS

Boasberg, who was first appointed to the federal bench by former President Barack Obama in 2010, has become a flashpoint for Republicans and the White House for his role in several high-profile cases against Trump and his administration during his two non-consecutive stints at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.

It’s caused Trump to call for his impeachment and the Justice Department to file a misconduct claim against him.

Boasberg most recently blocked the State Department from restricting visas for foreign officials and other foreign nationals that the administration has accused of suppressing or helping suppress American free speech.

SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS

That latest move is just the tip of the iceberg in a long-running set of clashes between Boasberg and Trump.

Boasberg has been a key player in the administration’s attempt to deport Venezuelan migrants. He tried to temporarily block the administration’s fast-paced deportation of Venezuelan migrants that the White House alleged were Tren de Aragua gang members.

He later ordered the administration that the men had to be returned to the U.S. for violating due process in their removal.

Boasberg also landed the case surrounding "Signalgate," where top members of Trump’s Cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance, War Secretary Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and then-National Security Advisor Michael Waltz, among others, accidentally included a journalist in their encrypted group message discussing strikes in Yemen.

He ordered the administration to preserve any of the messages related to the group chat, but stopped short of requiring that the administration salvage any that may have been deleted.

Schmitt hopes that his legislation will create a new operating standard moving forward.

"The BOASBERG Act prevents judges from forcing their way onto cases and is an important piece of court transparency legislation that will help restore the American people's confidence in our judiciary," Schmitt said.

item.title: Rahm Emanuel warns DSA agenda doesn't play well outside 'upper west side of Manhattan'
item.description: Former Obama chief of staff Rahm Emanuel claimed the Democratic Socialists of America's agenda could hand President Donald Trump a victory in the midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
Ex-White House chief of staff to former President Barack Obama, Rahm Emanuel, said Monday that the agenda put forth by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) does not appeal to anyone outside Manhattan ahead of November's midterm elections.

Emanuel's comments followed his Wall Street Journal opinion column last week warning that "Bernie bros" and democratic socialist candidates could threaten the Democratic Party's chances in statewide and nationwide elections with unpopular policies.

He doubled down on CNN with his concerns, claiming that any election not focused on President Donald Trump would be a "dollar wasted" for Democrats.

RAHM EMANUEL WARNS NEW GENERATION OF DEM SOCIALISTS DON'T LIKE AMERICA

"This election is set up to be a referendum on Donald Trump’s corruption and his inability to manage the economy to make people‘s lives better," Emanuel said. "Anything that distracts from that means you‘re helping Donald Trump. The DSA, and that agenda it's laid out, does not play anywhere except for maybe on the upper west side of Manhattan. And any time a Democrat anywhere in a red to blue district has to either distinguish themselves rather than prosecute that the Republican would be a rubber stamp for Donald Trump is a dollar wasted."

He specifically called out DSA-backed candidates for focusing on replacing Democratic candidates in safe districts rather than putting forth effort to win races in red or purple states like North Carolina, Georgia, Arizona and Nevada.

"Do you think anybody in those states wants a member of the DSA to come campaign or any of the Progressive Caucus? And second, since 2018, the progressive caucus hasn‘t flipped a single red to blue district. And to me, this is a consequential election where we could put a checkmate on Donald Trump, and we cannot risk it with diversions from the Democratic Socialists of America, who are giving them nothing but talking points," Emanuel said.

RAHM EMANUEL SPARS WITH NEW YORKER INTERVIEWER WHO GRILLED HIM FOR NOT EMPHASIZING TRANS ISSUES

Emanuel was also asked to respond to Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who criticized Emanuel as part of the Democratic "establishment" beholden to billionaire donors.

"You have an establishment like Rahm Emanuel, who are dependent on billionaire campaign contributors and want to maintain the status quo. Then you have a progressive movement, which, by the way, what is getting these guys nervous is we are winning all over this country. It’s not only Mamdani in New York City, it is in New Jersey, it’s in Ohio. It’s in Colorado. People are sick and tired of the ‘Rahm Emanuel’s’ and the Democratic establishment and the Republican establishment," Sanders said on "Face the Nation" Sunday.

Emanuel agreed with Sanders that "the system is rigged" against the middle class but emphasized that it was more important to take action rather than "talk about it."

"As I always say, the first eight letters of progressive spell 'progress,' not perfection. A lot of hot air out of Washington, not a lot of action out of it," Emanuel said.

DEM REP HENRY CUELLAR REJECTS DSA AGENDA, SAYS SOCIALISTS ARE TRYING TO 'USE' DEMOCRATIC PARTY

Fox News Digital reached out to Sanders' office and the DSA for comment.

In Emanuel's column, he blamed democratic socialist candidates for pushing unpopular positions that contributed to more moderate Democrats' losses.

"It was socialists who led the charge to defund the police, open the borders, abolish prisons, release violent criminals onto the streets and degrade the flag," Emanuel said.

Emanuel has a history of calling out the far-left on cultural issues that he thinks don’t play with the country at large. As Fox News Digital previously noted, the prominent Democrat said his party needed to stop alienating voters by talking down to them and fixating on niche identity politics issues. 

"We lost the plot," he said in a snippet shown on social media from the "Fifth Column" podcast in April. "We as Democrats nationally, from ‘Latinx,’ to defunding the police, to ‘Police organizations are all racist,’ to bringing a set of cultural wars to our schools. We are on the losing side of those cultural wars. Full stop."

In July, he sparred with a New Yorker interviewer over Democrats focusing on bathroom laws: "When people's backs are against the wall, they're holding on to that windowsill, and they can't make a college payment, they can't make a home mortgage payment, their healthcare is now being denied to them. They expect us Democrats to show up," he warned. 

"And we're showing up talking about bathroom access, sporting events, who gets to participate?"

item.title: The welfare state broke Black families. Work can help restore the dream
item.description: Fatherlessness and dependency grew by design as welfare punished families for keeping fathers in the home, breaking the Black family for generations.
item.content:encoded:
Recently, I heard Christian Maxwell, the Republican nominee for Illinois’ 1st Congressional District, say something that I’ve been thinking about ever since. She argued that the minute Black women start seeing themselves as Americans, as fully part of the American story, the entire progressive coalition built on grievances will begin to fall apart.

Her point was that Black women have been trained, indoctrinated and propagandized to see themselves as victims of America, and that’s why progress has been stifled. They’ve been rallying around sinister influences, especially false narratives about what a Black woman is, and that’s kept them locked in a culture of poverty and resentment instead of possibility and opportunity. She’s right. And I’ve spent the past 20 years on the South Side of Chicago watching how this has happened.

In plain words, what has happened has been nothing less than a divorce. I’m not talking about marriage, but the divorce between the Black woman and the American Dream.

I say Black woman here, not to single her out, but because it is a fact. Black women have been targeted by the United States government and nonprofits over the last 60 years in ways that no other race has been.

BOB WOODSON TAUGHT ME AMERICA’S WOUNDS HEAL ONLY THROUGH TRUTH AND COURAGE

All of this happened slowly and by design. The War on Poverty promised that we would be helped, and that government programs would lift us up. But, as Shelby Steele said in "What Killed Michael Brown?" the government that had oppressed us only yesterday would now become the agent of our own uplift. There was something sinister in what he said, and he was right. Why would we expect our former oppressor to lead us to the Promised Land? Isn’t it the oppressor’s main goal to alleviate his own guilt, and would we be used in that regard?

One of the bad ideas to come out of that war was the set of rules that punished a mother for keeping a man in the house and rewarded her financially for having more children without one. We called this assistance while fatherlessness shot through the roof. What it really was was an incentive to break up the family. And it worked, as generation after generation was born into this life of dependency. It wasn’t because these families were weak, but because the system promoted dependency as the safest and most responsible choice a mother could make.

Seeing the repercussions of these policies and the continual breakdown of families saddens me. I have never met a stronger woman than a single mother raising four kids on the South Side. These women didn’t choose this system. They were born into it, and my anger has never been at them. My anger is at a bureaucracy that asked them to trust it more than they trusted themselves.

MY WALK ACROSS AMERICA IS OVER, BUT MY MISSION FOR SOUTH SIDE KIDS IS NOT

That's the work of Project H.O.O.D. We're not in the business of judgment. We're in what I call the leap business. We help mothers move from a government check that keeps them small and dependent to a paycheck that makes them whole and independent. And let me tell you, that gap is real, and I believe the government creates it on purpose to keep people trapped. Sometimes this gap is $20,000 — money that a mother has to make on her own before independence pays better than dependency. That's not only a leap of faith, but a leap toward earning more and making capitalism work for you.

I've watched a mother of four sit through electrician training and come out with a job at an electrical contracting company. Others are planning to open their own businesses. I've watched a mother of two fail the police exam twice before she passed. She now wears the badge and has become one of the best officers on her beat. I didn't do that. They did that. All we did was stand at the bottom of the gap, provide the services and resources, and then say, "We believe you can make it across."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

And when they do, when that faith shows them what they are capable of and how much God has blessed them, I’m telling you, there is no look on a human face like it. Does anyone celebrate when they get a welfare check? No, but they sure celebrate when they get that paycheck, when they get an apartment of their own choosing and when they go out to a restaurant and treat themselves to a good meal. That's an American story.

That's why I believe in the trades. That's why I believe in reconnecting the Black woman and the Black family to the American Dream. That isn't charity. It's the restoration of what was already ours before the government decided it knew better.

Christian Maxwell said it plainly: The moment Black women fall in love with this country, this nation unifies like never before. I believe that too. They are the force. May God make them the force for a new day in America.

item.title: Battleground Democrat flip-flops on conversion therapy after left-wing backlash
item.description: Rebecca Cooke reversed her stance on a federal conversion therapy ban after progressive backlash, raising viability questions in the key swing district.
item.content:encoded:
A Democratic House candidate vying to flip a key Republican-held seat is on the defensive after reversing her position on conversion therapy following backlash from the party's left flank.

Rebecca Cooke, a Democratic challenger vying to unseat Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wis., repeatedly declined to endorse a federal ban on conversion therapy during several forums held ahead of the Aug. 11 primary.

But after drawing criticism from some progressive voters, Cooke reversed course, saying the federal government should prohibit the controversial practice, which often involves mental health professionals offering talk therapy for individuals struggling with their sexual orientation or gender identity.

The issue gained renewed attention when the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that Colorado could not enforce a state-level ban on conversion therapy over free speech concerns, sparking backlash from some Democrats.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME

The reversal comes as Cooke appears to be walking a political tightrope on LGBTQ issues in the Trump-friendly swing district, where she must appeal to both Democratic primary voters and the broader electorate.

Before Cooke can seek a rematch against Van Orden, she must first overcome a primary challenge from former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge, who is running to her left.

Asked what lawmakers could do to push back against the Supreme Court ruling at a May forum in La Crosse, Cooke sidestepped the question and said she preferred "local communities having control."

"I’m in favor of that sort of local control when making policies like this," the Wisconsin Democrat said.

Wisconsin’s conversion therapy ban took effect in 2022, while the city of Eau Claire, in Van Orden’s district, prohibited the practice in 2018.

Meanwhile, at a June candidate forum in Platteville, Cooke said "no" when asked if the federal government should pass legislation to ban conversion therapy.

Her answers prompted outrage from some progressive voters.

"I find it interesting that not in one, but TWO forums you said you would leave conversion therapy up to the states to decide," one user wrote on Facebook. "That is not protecting the LGBTQ community."

"I don’t know how you can say ‘Happy Pride’ if you aren’t willing to stand up for people you want to represent in Congress," another account replied. "If you are willing to sell out the LGBTQIA+ community for votes, who is next?"

CHRISTIAN COUNSELORS CHALLENGE WISCONSIN CONVERSION THERAPY BAN AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING

Amid the backlash, Cooke said she "misunderstood" the moderator's question and said she supported a federal ban on conversion therapy in a statement posted on a third-party account after the debate.

During a July forum in Eau Claire, Cooke clarified, "I do not support conversion therapy whatsoever."

Berge, who helped enact Eau Claire’s local conversion therapy ban, was clear throughout the candidate forums in denouncing the practice.

"As a therapist, conversion therapy has no place in our society, in our culture," she said during the June event.

Republicans sharply criticized Cooke’s reversal on conversion therapy bans.

Van Orden's campaign argued Cooke, who counts Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., among her endorsers, flip-flopped on her stance while still trying to "portray herself as a moderate."

"Rebecca Cooke is so desperate to appease the far-left woke mob that Wisconsin voters can’t be sure where she actually stands," Republican National Committee (RNC) spokesman Hunter Lovell told Fox News Digital.

"She’s trying to be one candidate for liberal activists and another for everyone else," he continued. "Whether it’s caving to the far left or scrambling to rebrand herself for the general election, Cooke owes Wisconsinites an answer: Which Rebecca Cooke would show up in Congress?"

Fox News Digital reached out to Cooke for comment.

Cooke, a former Democratic consultant, fundraiser and small business owner, has consistently supported expanding LGBTQ rights during her previous two failed bids for Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District.

In her third run for the seat, the repeat candidate is making clear that the Democrat-backed Equality Act — legislation that would make sexual orientation and gender identity protected classes under federal civil rights law potentially affecting women-only spaces and female sports teams — is a "centerpiece" of her campaign.

She is also endorsed by the progressive Human Rights Campaign, which has advocated for sex change procedures for minors, including hormone therapy and puberty blockers.

President Donald Trump comfortably carried the sprawling swing district by more than seven points in 2024, meaning Cooke would likely have to win over a segment of the president’s voters to prevail in November.

Cooke, who significantly outperformed former Vice President Kamala Harris, lost to Van Orden in the general election by just under three points in 2024, according to analysis from The Downballot.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the battleground contest as a "toss-up."

item.title: '80s icon Kristy McNichol makes rare appearance 25 years after leaving Hollywood
item.description: Kristy McNichol, who retired from Hollywood in 2001 after starring in "Family" and "Empty Nest," was spotted in a rare new photo with Carnie Wilson.
item.content:encoded:
Famous '80s icon Kristy McNichol made a rare appearance this week in a new photo with Carnie Wilson — 25 years after leaving Hollywood.

On July 20, the 58-year-old Wilson Philips singer shared a selfie on Facebook in which she was seen with the 63-year-old retired actress and gushed over her encounter with one of her childhood idols.

"Totally fangirling!!!" Wilson wrote in the caption. "Kris (Kristy McNichol) was a part of my youth. I adored her in her movies... Especially Little Darlings and The End."

Wilson went on to say that she told McNichol "how meaningful" her movies were to her and her close friend Tiffany Miller. The five-time Grammy Award nominee said she also shared that she and Miller were "JUST TALKING" about McNichol and "how special she is."

HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE

"What a gracious sweetie," Wilson added with a string of red heart emojis. "She sure is loved."

In the photo, McNichol was seen wearing a navy blue and red fleece jacket over a white T-shirt along with gold earrings. Wilson was clad in a black top with a brightly colored leaf pattern and a black beanie. The pair beamed as they stood close together and posed for the camera.

MELISSA GILBERT, MICHAEL LANDON AND MORE: WHERE THE ORIGINAL 'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' CAST IS NOW

McNichol launched her career as a child actor, starring in commercials and making guest appearances in hit sitcoms including "Starsky & Hutch," "CHiPs" and "The Love Boat."

The actress landed her first role as a series regular when she starred as Patricia Apple in the CBS drama series "Apple's Way" for two seasons from 1974 to 1975.

SALLY FIELD SAYS BURT REYNOLDS WAS ‘WONDERFUL’ BUT ‘FRIGHTENING,’ CLAIMS HE TRIED TO CONTROL HER CAREER

McNichol made her breakthrough in 1976 at age 14, when she was tapped to play Letitia "Buddy" Lawrence in the ABC drama series "Family." The role earned her two Primetime Emmy Awards and launched her as one of television's biggest teen stars.

BO DEREK REVEALS WHY SHE FELT LIKE AN 'IMPOSTOR' AND WALKED AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD DESPITE BLOCKBUSTER FAME

In 1977, McNichol began acting in movies and starred in the 1978 black comedy "The End" with Burt Reynolds and Sally Field. She won critical acclaim when she starred as Angel Bright in the hit 1980 teen comedy-drama "Little Darlings" alongside Tatum O'Neal, Matt Dillon and Armand Assante.

McNichol went on to star in the hit movies "The Night the Lights Went Out in Georgia" (1980) and "Only When I Laugh" (1981), the latter of which earned her a Golden Globe nomination for best supporting actress.

She also played leading roles in "The Pirate Movie" (1982), "Dream Lover" (1986) and "You Can't Hurry Love" (1988).

In 1986, she returned to TV full-time with a starring role on the sitcom "Empty Nest," which was a spin-off of the iconic sitcom "The Golden Girls." McNichol made her last on-screen appearance in the 1995 season finale of "Empty Nest" after stepping away from the show in 1992.

In 2001, McNichol announced that she was retiring from acting. "A lot of people have wondered what I've been up to," she said in a statement. "I retired from my career after 24 years."

"My feeling was that it was time to play my biggest part – myself!" McNichol continued. "I must say that it has been the best thing that ever happened to me. So many fans are disappointed that I'm not currently acting; however, some may not realize that the process I'm in at this time is necessary and vital for my personal happiness and well-being."

Since leaving the entertainment industry, McNichol has largely stayed out of the public eye. During a rare interview with People magazine in 2014, McNichol explained that she left Hollywood to "see what else was out there."

"I was on the big stage between ages 8 and 30," McNichol said. "I left show business for a variety of reasons, but a big one was my interest in learning what else there is in life."

"This phase of my life is so good," she shared. "My home life is happy and serene. I love singing. I also enjoy traveling and seeing the world. One of my favorite stops is Hawaii. I like everything about it and may eventually move there part-time."

While speaking with the outlet, McNichol did not rule out eventually making an acting comeback.

"Never say never," she said.

item.title: Ex-Biden campaign manager says there's 'no saving' DNC Chair Ken Martin after inside reports
item.description: Former Biden deputy campaign manager Rufus Gifford wrote that Ken Martin's DNC chairmanship cannot be saved as the committee spirals "toward irrelevance."
item.content:encoded:
Rufus Gifford, ex-deputy campaign manager to former President Joe Biden, explained on Monday why there is "no saving" Democratic National Committee (DNC) Chairman Ken Martin ahead of November's midterm elections.

Gifford, who served as DNC finance director during former President Barack Obama's administration, warned in a Substack article that the committee is "spiraling toward irrelevance" based on its inability to raise money and push its message, largely based on Martin's unwillingness to communicate compared to his predecessors.

"The number of times Jim Messina or Jen O’Malley Dillon called me to help try and figure out how to fund special projects like these are in the dozens," Gifford explained in the article. "And we were successful because of the relationships we had collectively built and the trust we had accumulated over the years."

STATES MAY DEFY DNC PRIMARY CALENDAR AS 'NOBODY IS SCARED' OF KEN MARTIN, CNN REPORTER SAYS

He added, "It seems clear that such requests or the multitude of others – and there will be literally hundreds of asks for money in the fall – could not be met with a 'yes' at this point. That is a failure and we have been seeing this coming for a year now."

Though Gifford clarified that he believed Martin to be "a good man," he wrote that he never heard from the DNC head during his time with Biden in 2024, further proving that he was unable to rise to the occasion.

"At this point, I think there is no saving Martin’s chairmanship. He is a good man with good intentions but simply not meeting this critical moment. The leaks coming from inside the building streaming across every media outlet say to me that the (diligent and wonderful) staff are losing or have lost faith," Gifford wrote. 

JOE SCARBOROUGH GOES OFF ON 'HORRIBLE' DNC CHAIR, 'CRAZY' DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN SCATHING ON-AIR CRITIQUE

He continued, "As Democrats, the only solution is to acknowledge the problem and fix it. Now. We need to lean on each other, call each other for help, acknowledge the anger and the disappointment people feel while respecting and bringing together the voices both new and old."

item.title: Russia exposes NATO weapons gap as top commander warns ‘the math is not in favor of the West’
item.description: NATO's top transformation commander says the West cannot produce enough Patriot missiles and must redesign its entire weapons industrial base.
item.content:encoded:
Days after NATO allies committed tens of billions of dollars to new air and missile defenses, the alliance’s top transformation commander warned that the West must fundamentally redesign its weapons and industrial base to withstand attacks at the scale now being demonstrated in Ukraine and the Middle East.

"Today, the math is not in favor of the West," Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation (SACT), told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview following the alliance’s summit in Ankara, Turkey, in early July.

The summit produced commitments to acquire 900 Patriot missiles and invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities throughout five years. 

But Vandier argued that simply buying more of the West’s existing weapons will not solve the underlying problem.

TRUMP ENTERS FINAL NATO SUMMIT DAY AS UKRAINE, DEFENSE SPENDING TAKE CENTER STAGE

Russia’s nightly barrages against Ukraine have exposed an air-defense model designed for smaller numbers of incoming threats. The U.S.-Iran conflict has simultaneously intensified demand for the high-end interceptors needed to defeat ballistic missiles, including Patriots and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) that cannot quickly be replaced.

"There is no way to produce 50,000 Patriots a year," Vandier said. "We don’t have the supply chain, and it’s not worth doing that given the cost of the weapon."

Instead, Vandier said NATO needs a layered mix of defenses: cheaper weapons that can be mass-produced to counter waves of drones, while preserving advanced interceptors for ballistic missiles and other sophisticated threats.

THE TWO MOST IMPORTANT AMERICAN WEAPONS SYSTEMS NATO IS EAGER TO HAVE

"You need to have attritable, low-cost, mass-produced weapons to just kill the low-cost weapons that are coming by big waves," Vandier said. "And then you need still the exquisite, complex weapons to kill the most complex weapons, as ballistic missiles."

Trump announced at the summit that the United States would grant Ukraine a license to manufacture Patriot interceptors, potentially allowing Kyiv to build more of the weapons it urgently needs to defend against Russian ballistic missiles.

But asked whether the announcement changed his assessment that Patriots alone could not protect Europe throughout the next five years, Vandier pointed to a deeper obstacle: Western weapons were designed around an industrial base that no longer exists.

UKRAINE’S BATTLEFIELD IS TRANSFORMING THE FUTURE OF NATO

"The design needs to change," Vandier said. "We are at a moment where some stuff will be redesigned under pressure to be mass-produced."

NATO also is attempting to transform against a threat that is changing in real time. Asked about a recent Russian live-fire exercise on Lake Peipus, between Estonia and Russia, which Estonia’s defense minister assessed was likely practice against Ukrainian-style naval drones, Vandier said Russia has demonstrated an ability to absorb battlefield lessons and adjust "on a weekly basis."

"War — if you do not adapt, you die," Vandier said. "All your brain is about how you outmatch, outpace, outrun the enemy. And so Russia is not that bad at that."

"For NATO now, it’s a question of speed of adaptation," Vandier said. "It’s a mind game."

Ukraine’s defense industry, meanwhile, is increasingly setting the pace for the larger Western manufacturers that once supplied most of its weapons, Vandier said. Ukrainian companies have been able to develop, field and modify systems quickly in response to changes on the battlefield.

"The very agile and fast-evolving industrial base in Ukraine is now giving the pace to the European and Western industry," Vandier said.

But the technological competition is not confined to drones and air defenses. Vandier warned that the collapse of the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty has reopened a broader race over long-range missiles in Europe, as Russia and NATO allies seek weapons capable of holding targets farther behind enemy lines at risk.

The 1987 treaty prohibited the United States and Russia from possessing ground-launched missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometers. The first Trump administration withdrew from the agreement in 2019 after accusing Moscow of violating it, an allegation Russia denied.

Vandier said the disappearance of those limits has produced a period of "complete strategic instability," with both sides under pressure to develop new capabilities to preserve deterrence.

"The Pandora’s box is open again," Vandier said, "and we’ll try to close it down one day."

item.title: WATCH: Rand Paul says Fauci lobbied for $1M prize while leading COVID response
item.description: Rand Paul claims Anthony Fauci lobbied NIH colleagues to nominate him for the $1 million Dan David Prize while serving as White House medical advisor.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., wants answers from former chief White House medical advisor Anthony Fauci on why he used his rising fame to lobby colleagues to nominate him for a $1 million prize.

Paul, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, is gearing up for a blockbuster hearing with Fauci, the former head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), for his role as spokesman and policy craftsman during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Ahead of the hearing, Paul dumped over 1,000 pages of Fauci’s diary, and he told Fox News Digital that one of the issues that would soon come to light during Wednesday’s fight in the Senate was Fauci’s alleged dogged pursuit of a hefty cash prize while serving under former President Joe Biden.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

"We have conversations where he's telling other people at the NIH to nominate him," Paul said. "Like, ‘Will you nominate me? I'll write up my nominating background for you, and then you nominate me.’"

"Why would we let — politicians aren't supposed to get more than $50," he continued. "Why would we let a guy that runs a bureaucracy, why would we want him to be allowed to have a $1 million prize? That just boggles my mind."

In 2021, Fauci was awarded the Dan David Prize, a $1 million award disbursed by the Israel-based Dan David Foundation headquartered at Tel Aviv University. Per the rules of the award, 10% of the prize was meant to be designated for academic scholarships in Fauci’s field.

LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION NEARS FINISH LINE AS WORLD LEADERS GATHER TO HONOR HIM

The foundation said in a statement at the time that as the pandemic unraveled, Fauci "leveraged his considerable communication skills to address people gripped by fear and anxiety and worked relentlessly to inform individuals in the United States and elsewhere about the public health measures essential for containing the pandemic’s spread."

Despite advising seven presidents and serving at the NIH since the 1980s, Fauci was a career civil servant who never required Senate confirmation.

Strewn across the pages of Fauci’s diary are several instances, particularly in the early stages of the pandemic, that show an individual with a keen understanding of his role in the media.

FAUCI'S DIARY SHOWS HE FED QUESTIONS TO JOURNALISTS, BUILT FRIENDSHIPS WITH MEDIA FIGURES

In May 2020, for example, Fauci wrote that a "Big front page article [about] me appeared in the Washington Post."

"Very flattering. The situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable," he said. "It is not [hyperbole] to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable [persons] in the world."

And in another entry shortly after, Fauci noted that the Trump White House was "very upset" about his meteoric rise in the media.

When asked about Fauci's close eye on the media and whether that might have colored his portrayal of the virus, Paul was unsure.

"I mean, he wouldn't be the first person in Washington that publicity went to his head," Paul said.

item.title: Rosie O'Donnell accuses CBS of giving Trump a 'bribe' by settling '60 Minutes' lawsuit
item.description: Rosie O'Donnell said CBS gave President Donald Trump a "bribe" with its $16 million "60 Minutes" settlement, echoing Stephen Colbert's criticism of the deal.
item.content:encoded:
Liberal comedian Rosie O'Donnell accused CBS of "capitulating" to President Donald Trump on Monday during "The View" co-host Ana Navarro's podcast, saying the network's $16 million settlement of his "60 Minutes" lawsuit was a "bribe" that undermined an independent press.

Appearing on "Bleep! with Ana Navarro," O'Donnell invoked former CBS late-night host Stephen Colbert, who used similar language while criticizing the agreement on his show last year.

"[CBS] capitulated. They did exactly what Stephen Colbert said they did," O’Donnell said. "They gave him a bribe and it’s unforgivable."

ROSIE O'DONNELL CLAIMS TRUMP HAS 'PTSD RESPONSE' TO HER AS BACKLASH ERUPTS

O'Donnell said the agreement demonstrated why she believed the country no longer had a sufficiently independent media establishment to scrutinize the government.

"We need a very vibrant, alive, independent media," O’Donnell said. "And we no longer have it in this country."

The CBS case concerned the network's editing of an October 2024 "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump accused CBS of deceptively editing Harris' answer about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to benefit her before the presidential election.

Paramount Global and CBS settled the lawsuit in July 2025 for $16 million, covering legal costs and a contribution to Trump's future presidential library or charitable causes. The agreement contained no apology or admission of journalistic wrongdoing, and no money was paid directly to Trump.

Trump’s legal team portrayed the settlement as a victory over the media.

"CBS and Paramount Global realized the strength of this historic case and had no choice but to settle," a Trump legal spokesperson said at the time.

SHARYN ALFONSI OUT AT ’60 MINUTES' AFTER FEUD WITH BARI WEISS, RIPS CBS FOR ‘CHILLING MESSAGE’ TO NEWSROOM

During the discussion with Navarro on Monday, O'Donnell referred to Trump as a "convicted sexual rapist" while explaining why she moved to Ireland following his 2024 election victory. Navarro cautioned her against the description, prompting O'Donnell to turn to CBS and its settlement.

Trump was not criminally convicted of rape. A civil jury found him liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll. ABC News separately agreed to pay $15 million toward Trump’s future presidential foundation or museum after anchor George Stephanopoulos repeatedly said Trump had been found liable for rape.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and CBS for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

TRUMP THREATENS TO ADD NY TIMES' 'TREASONOUS' IRAN WAR COVERAGE TO $15B DEFAMATION LAWSUIT

Colbert criticized the CBS settlement with Trump on "The Late Show" last year because Paramount was awaiting federal approval of its multibillion-dollar merger with Skydance Media.

"I believe this kind of complicated financial settlement with a sitting government official has a technical name in legal circles. It’s ‘big fat bribe,’" Colbert said.

CBS announced three days later it would cancel "The Late Show" at the end of the 2025-2026 season, calling the move a financial decision unrelated to Colbert's content or other developments at Paramount. 

"It is not related in any way to the show’s performance, content or other matters happening at Paramount," CBS said in a July 2025 press release.

Colbert hosted the program's final episode in May.

The Federal Communications Commission approved Skydance’s $8 billion acquisition of Paramount three weeks after the settlement. The merger closed in August 2025. Paramount maintained during the proceedings that Trump’s lawsuit was "completely separate from, and unrelated to, the Skydance transaction and the FCC approval process."

item.title: We all are desperate for a financial check-up. Time to say, ‘Show me the money!’
item.description: A simple Money BMI checklist reveals whether you're financially fit or financially out of shape, measuring emergency fund, debt reduction and retirement savings.
item.content:encoded:
Every year, millions of Americans step on a scale to see if they're healthy.

They check their weight. They know their blood pressure. They monitor cholesterol. Many even wear smartwatches that track every heartbeat and every step they take.

JENNIE GARTH ADMITS ‘SCARY’ FINANCIAL SPIRAL AFTER ‘90210’ FAME

But here's a question almost nobody can answer:

The truth is, America has no simple way to measure financial wellness. We know our credit score. We know our bank balance. We may even know what our 401(k) is worth.

But none of those numbers answer the question that really matters.

Years ago, I introduced the idea of a Money BMI because I believed Americans needed a financial version of the Body Mass Index, a simple measurement that tells you whether you're on the right track before small problems become major ones.

Think about it. Doctors don’t wait until someone has a heart attack before talking about exercise. They measure warning signs early.

Our financial system should work the same way.

Today, too many Americans discover they're financially unhealthy only after a crisis. A layoff. A divorce. A market correction. An unexpected medical bill. Retirement arriving years sooner than expected.

By then, fixing the problem becomes much harder.

Instead of asking only, "How much money do you have?" we should be asking better questions.

Do you have an emergency fund? Are you saving at least 15% of your income? Could your family survive financially if something happened to you? Do you have a current estate plan? Are you paying unnecessary taxes? Will your retirement savings actually provide enough income?

Those questions paint a far more accurate picture of financial health than a brokerage statement ever could.

Imagine if every American had a simple annual Financial Fitness Score that could be something as recognizable as stepping on a scale at the doctor's office.

Not another government program. Not another complicated regulation. Not a new retirement plan you need an engineering degree to figure out.

Just a practical way to identify financial risks before they become financial emergencies.

Here's a quick version of what I call your Money BMI Check:

If you checked five or six boxes, you're probably in strong financial shape.

Three or four? You're making progress but have work to do.

Two or fewer? Your financial health deserves immediate attention, and you might be considered financially obese, just as your physical health would if your doctor raised similar concerns.

The good news is that financial fitness isn't reserved for the wealthy. Just like physical fitness, it improves through consistent habits rather than dramatic changes.

Small increases in savings. Reducing debt. Reviewing insurance. Updating estate documents. Automating good financial decisions. Over time, those habits compound into lasting financial security.

America has spent decades encouraging people to build wealth. We've done far less to help people measure whether they're actually on track. Great leaders will always tell you, "Expect what you inspect." Why don’t we have a mandatory inspection system for your Money BMI?

Maybe it's time we changed that.

Because just as knowing your physical BMI won't automatically make you healthier, knowing your Money BMI won't automatically make you wealthier.

But it may be the wake-up call that changes your financial future before it's too late.

item.title: Trump welcomes Netanyahu to White House as raging Iran war threatens to sour US-Israel relationship

item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump will welcome Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to the White House Tuesday for talks that could shape the next phase of the U.S. standoff with Iran.

A political shadow is cast over the visit, however, amid renewed calls from the far-left to arrest the Israeli leader.

"Every meeting between Prime Minister Netanyahu and President Trump has carried drama and historic weight, but this one comes as the Middle East stands at a genuine crossroads," Shurat HaDin Law Center President Nitsana Darshan-Leitner told Fox News Digital of the upcoming sit-down.

"The decisions made by these two leaders in Washington will have far-reaching repercussions and will determine not only the next chapter in confronting Iran, but whether the region moves toward lasting stability or slips back into dangerous and chaotic escalation," added Darshan-Leitner.

NETANYAHU TO VISIT TRUMP AT WHITE HOUSE, ATTEND 'DEAR FRIEND' LINDSEY GRAHAM'S MEMORIAL SERVICE

Netanyahu is in Washington, D.C., to attend the funeral service of Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., whom he has called a dear friend not just to Israel, but to himself. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is also in D.C. for the funeral of the late senator and is using the opportunity to meet with Trump. 

The high-stakes talks between the world leaders come as Israel continues to press for a tougher Iran strategy, while Trump is weighing whether to resume major strikes against Iran.

"He's been a great wartime prime minister," Trump told reporters Wednesday, speaking of Netanyahu. "We worked with each other very closely. And we went through a very big thing. We did a big thing together."

The Israeli leader’s visit has stirred controversy over Israel’s handling of Gaza as well as its approach to Iran.

MAMDANI GOES BACK ON CAMPAIGN PROMISE, SAYS NYC CAN'T ARREST NETANYAHU

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called on the federal government to carry out the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant ahead of a possible Netanyahu visit to the Big Apple for the United Nations General Assembly in September.

Former Mayor Bill de Blasio defended Mamdani’s call to have Netanyahu arrested, stating the Israeli leader is "fomenting hate."

The relationship between longtime allies Trump and Netanyahu — who is often referred to as Bibi — appeared to face a rare rift over their differing views in the two countries' handling of the conflict with Iran.

TRUMP CONFIRMS ‘CRAZY’ NETANYAHU CLASH AS QUESTIONS MOUNT OVER PUSH TO HOLD FIRE ON HEZBOLLAH TERRORISTS

Trump admitted that he called Netanyahu "f---ing crazy" in a heated phone call over Israel’s military operations in Lebanon.

"So many in the media attempt to portray deep rifts between the President and the Prime Minister while they need to project unity and strength," Darshan-Leitner explained to Fox News Digital. "History will likely remember this meeting not simply for what was discussed behind closed doors, but for the course it set for the region — and perhaps the world — for years to come."

Netanyahu is expected to present Trump with intelligence in their meeting on Tuesday alleging Iran is expanding activity at its Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site and is not negotiating in good faith over its nuclear program, according to the New York Post, citing a source in Jerusalem.

Trump delayed planned U.S. military strikes against Iran for several days while emphasizing that the United States remains prepared to launch a "massive attack," if necessary.

Trump said Monday Washington is engaged in "good talks" with Iran, but warned that if negotiations fail, the U.S. would resume military action.

"From the future of Iran’s nuclear ambitions, to the security of U.S. bases, to the ownership of the Strait of Hormuz and the freedom of global maritime commerce, the stakes extend far beyond Israel’s borders," said Darshan-Leitner. "This is one of the rare moments when diplomacy and deterrence must move in lockstep."

item.title: DNA cracks centuries-old murder mystery involving one of history's most famous families
item.description: Ancient DNA from the Medici brothers' remains revealed a novel malaria strain, offering scientific proof against longstanding poisoning rumors, researchers say.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers at Yale University believe they've solved a centuries-old mystery over how a member of one of Italy's most famous families died.

In a study published in the journal iScience, researchers analyzed ancient DNA from Grand Duke Francesco I de' Medici, the Renaissance ruler of Tuscany, who died suddenly in 1587.

Francesco I de' Medici and his wife, Bianca Cappello, died a day apart after falling ill with intermittent fevers following a stay at a mosquito-filled villa — fueling centuries of rumors that they had been poisoned.

EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

Working with paleopathologists from the University of Pisa in Italy, the team analyzed DNA extracted from the ribs of Francesco I de' Medici, as well as Giovanni de' Medici, his younger brother who died of malaria 25 years earlier.

The research was led by Serena Tucci, assistant professor of anthropology at Yale University, whose work was publicized in a university press release on June 30.

Researchers found genetic traces of Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite responsible for the deadliest form of malaria — effectively debunking the longstanding poisoning theory.

The team "found a novel strain of Plasmodium falciparum, the species that causes the deadliest form of human malaria, in the bones of Giovanni de Medici," the release said.

ANCIENT ROMAN VILLA BENEATH HIGH SCHOOL GYM REVEALS STUNNING SECRET FROM THE PAST

"The researchers also discovered molecular traces of P. falciparum and a second species, P. malariae, in the remains of Francesco de Medici," the statement added.

While malaria was endemic to central Italy during the Renaissance, the lack of definitive scientific evidence allowed theories to persist.

"Their quick deaths spawned rumors that Francesco’s brother and rival, Cardinal Ferdinando de Medici, had them poisoned with arsenic," said the statement.

It marks the first time researchers have genetically analyzed the brothers' skeletal remains, confirming earlier evidence they had malaria.

SHAKESPEARE'S MISSING LONDON HOME PINPOINTED AFTER CENTURIES-LONG MYSTERY, RESEARCHER SAYS

The results are "scientific proof to dispel persistent speculation that Francesco de Medici was poisoned to death," Yale officials said.

Archival sources, including contemporary reports from court physicians, describe the symptoms the brothers suffered that are consistent with malaria, which was called "febbre terzana" by residents of Central Italy at the time.

"The reports also describe the treatments to which the stricken were subjected, including bloodletting, a common practice that likely did patients more harm than good," the release said.

Although historical records described symptoms consistent with malaria, rumors that Francesco had been poisoned persisted for centuries, Tucci told Fox News Digital.
